ANSWERS
Case 1: Diagnosis: Respiratory Acidosis
Explanation: Look at the Flowchart 20.1. In this case, pH low and
PCO2 high, suggest it is respiratory acidosis. Now, calculate HCO3
–
to
assess compensation. HCO3
–
levels are higher by 2 mEq/L (for
increase PCO2 of 20 mm Hg) which may represent partial renal
compensation (full compensation will be around 8 to 10 mEq/L for
PCO2
 of
20 mm Hg). As history suggests it is an acute respiratory acidosis
which may be due to suppression of respiratory centers by some
substance abuse at party.
Case 2: Diagnosis: Metabolic Acidosis
Explanation: Look at the Flowchart 20.1. As the pH and HCO3
– value
suggest it is metabolic acidosis. Calculate expected PCO2 = 1.5 ×
[HCO3
–
] + 8±2 = 1.5 × 13 + 8 = 27.5 ± 2 This PCO2
represent
respiratory compensation. As history suggests it is a case of metabolic
acidosis due to diabetic ketoacidosis with respiratory compensation.
Case 3: Diagnosis: Respiratory Alkalosis
Explanation: Look at the Flowchart 20.2. As the pH and PCO2 value
suggest it is respiratory alkalosis. HCO3
–
levels are lower by 3 mEq/L
which may represent partial renal compensation. Full compensation
would have been of around 5 to
6 mEq/L for 12 mm Hg drop in PCO2
. (5 mEq/L for PCO2 of 10 mm
Hg). As history suggests it is an acute respiratory alkalosis due to
hyperventilation.
Case 4: Diagnosis: Metabolic Alkalosis
Explanation: Look at the Flowchart 20.2. As the pH and HCO3
– value
suggest it is metabolic alkalosis. The expected PaCO2 = 0.7 × ([HCO3
–
]
-24) + 40 ± 2 = 0.7 × (32 -24) + 40 = 45.5 which is almost same with
PCO2 value given. As history suggests it is a case of metabolic
alkalosis due to loss of acid by GI ailment with respiratory
compensation.
Case 5: Diagnosis: Combined respiratory acidosis and metabolic
acidosis.
Explanation: Low pH and high PCO2
indicate a respiratory acidosis
and the low blood [HCO3
–
] signifies a metabolic acidosis. The
respiratory acidosis is due to respiratory arrest and circulatory collapse
(decreased pulmonary ventilation and perfusion), and the metabolic
acidosis is a consequence of the associated tissue anoxia, i.e.
anaerobic glycolysis, with excessive production of peripheral lactic acid.
Case 6: Diagnosis: Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis.
Explanation: In this patient the respiratory alkalosis is due to
hyperventilation consequent to lobar pneumonia; the metabolic
alkalosis can be attributed to the thiazide-induced hypokalemia.
Although her blood [HCO3
–
] is only slightly above the upper reference
interval, before the onset of the metabolic alkalosis it would have been
several millimoles per liter lower, given that respiratory alkalosis
(chronic and acute) is associated with a compensatory decrease in the
plasma bicarbonate.
Case 7: Diagnosis: Read below.
Explanation: The levels of pH and HCO3
– are high, indicates
metabolic alkalosis. Now, calculate expected PaCO2
from Flowchart
20.2; PaCO2 = 0.7 × ([HCO3
–
] -24) + 40 ± 2 = (0.7× 38 - 24) + 40 ± 2 =
42.6 ± 2, So, we can understand that the PaCO2 did not increase as
expected, indicates the patient also had respiratory alkalosis, perhaps
because of stress or fever. The anion gap was 16 mmol/L; a much
higher value might be indicative of additional metabolic acidosis.
Also, metabolic alkalosis, particularly that which is caused by vomiting
or diuretic use, can be associated with an increment in the serum anion
gap of approximately 4 to 6 mmol/L.

options: b. Blood flow to apex of lung
d. Settling of carbon particles in the lung
questions.correct_answer: d. Settling of carbon particles in the lung
questions.explanation:
Microgravity or, 0 gravity does not permit the settling of airborne
particle like earth. This is because, sedimentation process is affected
most in 0 gravity condition. Deposition is an linear function of G level
for 2- and 3-μm particles and virtually absent in 0 gravity.
In the absence of gravity, venous blood will rush to the right
atrium because the force of gravity is no longer pulling the blood
down into the vessels of the legs and abdomen, resulting in
increased stroke volume.

questions.question: What happens in case of “Vasopressin escape” on SIADH?
options: d. Down regulation of Aquaporin 2 receptors
questions.correct_answer: d. Down regulation of Aquaporin 2 receptors
questions.explanation:
■ There is a process in where a significant number of lung tumors
and some other cancers secrete vasopressin called “vasopressin
escape”.
■ “Vasopressin escape” that counteracts the water-retaining
action of vasopressin to limit the degree of hyponatremia in
SIADH.
■ Vasopressin escape is characterized by a sudden increase in
urine volume with a decrease in urine osmolality independent of
circulating vasopressin levels.
■ Prolonged exposure to elevated levels of vasopressin can lead
eventually to down-regulation of the production of aquaporin-2.
■ This permits urine flow suddenly to increase and plasma
osmolality to fall despite exposure of the collecting ducts to
elevated levels of the hormone; that is, the individual escapes
from the renal effects of vasopressin.
